chunks: Musa ibn al-Qasim from Safwan and Ibn Abi Umayr from Rifa'ah ibn Musa said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who vowed to walk to the House of Allah (al-Haram); would that suffice for him as the Hajj of Islam? He said, 'Yes.' I said, 'What do you think if he performs Hajj on behalf of someone else, and he has no wealth, and he had vowed to perform Hajj on foot; would that suffice for him in place of his walking?' He said, 'Yes.'

And whoever upon whom the Hajj of Islam becomes obligatory, and he dies before reaching the Haram, then it is upon his guardian to fulfill it on his behalf from his estate. And if he dies after entering the Haram, that suffices for him. Narrated.
ai.seo_question: Does a vow to walk to Mecca suffice for the obligatory Hajj, and what happens if one dies before reaching the Haram?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies that a vow to perform Hajj on foot is legally sufficient to discharge the obligatory duty, emphasizing the validity of intention and method in Shia jurisprudence. It further extends this principle to cases of poverty and proxy performance, while establishing the heir's obligation to fulfill the deceased's unperformed Hajj from the estate if death occurred before entering the Miqat. This ruling underscores the flexibility within Shia fiqh regarding the fulfillment of religious vows and the continuity of obligations after death.
